units.spoken: Continuous-Action RL
When a robot must set real-numbered turning forces, not pick from a list.

sections.section: 1 Robot arms set real-numbered turning forces

units.spoken: Section one, Robot arms set real-numbered turning forces
1.1 A robot arm that turns at its joints

A robot arm must set real-numbered turning forces at its joints every step. This page shows why picking from a fixed list of choices, as the Deep Q-Network (DQN) does when it scores every choice and keeps the best, fails, and what every method that replaces it shares. A short list makes the arm jerky, and a fine one grows huge.

The agent is the learner that picks the moves. (RL Basics) A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad. (RL Basics) On a robot, sensing, moving and earning rewards repeat many times every second.

The running example is the Reacher task: a robot arm with two joints whose actions are four torques. A torque is a turning force a motor applies at a joint. On the Reacher each torque is a number from -1 to 1. Each joint can turn about two axes, so each joint gets two torques. Every step the arm senses its state, numbers describing the position, rotation and speed of its parts, and earns a small reward whenever its hand is inside a moving goal.

Take a look at this figure. The arm has two joints, and each joint turns on two axes, so the arm needs four torques, one per axis, every step. The hand earns its reward only while it stays inside the moving goal circle. That is the whole problem of this page in one picture: the action is a set of four real numbers, not a pick from a list, and the numbers have to land the hand in a moving target.

Figure 1 shows the Reacher arm, with two joints, four torques and a moving goal. The arm hangs from a base at the lower left, with a shoulder joint and an elbow joint, and two curved arrows at each joint, one per turning axis, so each joint gets two torques. Take the hand: it sits near the dashed green goal circle, and the arm earns its small reward whenever the hand stays inside that moving circle.

A continuous action is a real number, or a list of them, that can take any value in a range, like a torque, instead of one choice from a list. Each of the four torques can take any value in its range, so there is no list of choices to score.
1.2 A list of torque levels is jerky and huge

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. (RL Basics) A move's value Q of s and a, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes action a in state s and plays on from there. (RL Basics) A Q-table keeps one score for every state and move. (Q-Learning) The arm's joint angles and speeds can take endless values, so such a table could never list them all.

DQN swaps the table for a network. A Q-network is a neural network that takes the state and outputs one score per move, in place of the table. (Deep Q-Networks (DQN)) DQN plays the move with the best score.

On the arm, a list of moves can only come from chopping each torque into a few levels. Few levels make the arm move in jerks, and each extra torque multiplies the list, so it soon grows too long to search. A many-joint arm makes the same point: even a coarse list of levels per joint multiplies into a list far too long to search well.

Take a look at this figure. Chopping two torques into levels makes a grid, and more levels make the grid denser, so the arm can aim finer. But each extra level multiplies the list, and the other two torques multiply it again. The lesson is the trade: a coarse list is jerky, a fine list is huge, and no list is both smooth and short.

Figure 2 shows two grids of allowed torque levels for two torques. The left grid has few levels, three dots across and three down, and the right grid has many more, six across and six down, so it looks much denser. Take the right grid: each extra level on one torque multiplies the list again, and the other two torques multiply it once more, so the list soon grows too long to search.
Section two, What every continuous-action method shares
2.1 One network scores the state and the torques together

DDPG, TD3 and SAC use two networks. The critic Q sub phi is a network with weights phi that scores a state and an action together; its score stands for the return the agent expects. For the Reacher, the action is four torques. The critic takes the torques as an input, unlike DQN's one output per move in its list. So one network can score any torques the arm might send, even ones it has never tried. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is the exception: its critic guesses each state's value, and the advantage is how much better a move was than that guess.
2.2 A second network outputs the torques

A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. (RL Basics) Here the policy is a network that must output a whole set of real numbers. An actor is the policy network that picks the action; the critic's guesses are used to score how good it was. (Actor-Critic: A2C and A3C) The actor's torques go straight to the arm's motors at every step.

A deterministic actor outputs one set of torques every time. With no randomness of its own it would never try anything new, so exploring needs noise added from outside. Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) is the simplest actor-critic here. Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) adds a second critic and trusts the lower score. Both use this kind of actor. Such an actor is cheap to run on a robot, since it needs no random draw.

A stochastic actor draws its torques at random from a bell curve, most often near its centre. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) rewards its actor for keeping its bell of torques wide. It uses this kind. Either way, the actor's torques are the action the critic scores.
2.3 Learning from stored steps

Off-policy means learning the values of one policy while playing another. (SARSA: Learning the Value of the Moves You Play) For the off-policy methods here that means learning from steps an older version of the agent took. Replay keeps a memory of past steps, and training draws random batches from it. (Deep Q-Networks (DQN)) The critic trains on random batches of those stored steps, so it does not learn only from the arm's last few moves.

The critic learns by being pulled toward a target, the step's reward plus its own score for what comes next, counted a little less. That target moves whenever the critic moves. For the off-policy methods here, the target is built from slow copies of the critics. Each one moves only a little at a time toward its critic (Training DDPG shows how the copies update).

For DDPG, TD3 and SAC, the actor learns by changing its torques in the direction that raises the critic's score; the DDPG page shows how. PPO's actor learns differently, from advantages, and each update is clipped so the policy moves only a little.

Take a look at this figure. The state goes to the actor, the actor sends its torques to the arm, and the critic takes the state and the torques together and points back at the actor. That arrow is the whole trick: the critic's score tells the actor which way to change its torques so the score rises. The actor learns by following that arrow, one step at a time.

Figure 3 shows the state going to the actor, the torques going to the arm, and the critic telling the actor which way the score rises. Across the top the state feeds the actor, the actor feeds its torques to the arm, and below, the state and the torques both feed the critic, which points back up to the actor. Take one step on the Reacher: the actor sends four torques to the arm, and the critic's arrow shows which way to change them so the score rises.
The two lines below show the difference in code, and the name q net stands for the Q-network.

This code shows the difference in two lines. The first line asks the Q-network for the move with the best score, picking one entry from a list. The second line asks the actor for its torques and squashes each one into the torque range, from minus 1 to 1. One line lists, the other outputs.
1. Picks an entry from a list. Arg max picks the move whose score is largest. (RL Basics)
2. Gives four torques. In the torch library, tanh squashes any number into -1 to 1, the torque range.
Section three, Continuous-action methods side by side

PPO is another way to train an actor that draws its torques from a bell curve; it makes small, careful updates and learns only from fresh steps. The Q-critic methods differ mainly in how they keep the critic from scoring torques above the return the arm really earns, and how they explore.

Two of these methods keep two critics because a single critic tends to score some torques too high. DQN's target takes a max, the highest of the scores its Q-network gives the next moves. Overestimation means the values climb above the return the agent really earns, because a max over noisy guesses picks lucky ones. (Double DQN) In DDPG and TD3 the actor plays the role of the max, because it learns to pick the torques the critic scores highest; SAC's actor does the same while keeping its bell wide.

Multi-agent DDPG (MADDPG) trains several agents together, and each agent's critic sees what all the agents do. Here there is only one arm, so a single critic scores all of its moves. TD3 and SAC both train two critics and trust the lower of their two scores, and TD3 also updates its actor less often, so the critics' scores settle before the actor follows them. That wait is the Delayed in Twin Delayed DDPG.

This table lines up the five continuous-action methods side by side: what each one adds, its actor kind, its critics, and how it explores. Read across a row to see how one method works, and down a column to see how the methods differ. DDPG adds an actor that outputs the torques and a critic that scores them: its actor is deterministic, it keeps one critic, and it explores by adding noise from outside to its torques. TD3 adds a second critic and trusts the lower score, and its actor updates half as often as the critics: its actor is deterministic too, its target is built from the lower score, and it explores by adding noise from outside, drawn fresh each step. SAC adds a reward for keeping its bell of torques wide: its actor is stochastic, drawing its torques at random from a bell curve, it keeps two critics, and it explores by keeping that bell wide. PPO adds small, careful updates and learns only from fresh steps: its actor is stochastic, it keeps one critic, and it explores by drawing its torques at random from a bell curve. MADDPG adds several agents learning together, each agent's critic seeing what all the agents do: one actor per agent, one critic per agent, and each agent explores with noise added from outside. The pattern: the Q-critic methods differ in how they keep the critic from scoring too high, two critics and the lower score, and in how they explore, noise from outside or a wide bell.

Table 1 lines the five continuous-action methods up side by side, with what each one adds, its actor kind, its critics, and how it explores. Each row names one method, so a row reads as that method's whole shape: DDPG adds an actor and a critic, TD3 adds a second critic and trusts the lower score, SAC rewards a wide bell of torques. Take the SAC row: its actor draws torques at random from a bell curve, and it explores by keeping that bell wide.
Entropy H is how undecided the policy is; for a bell of torques, it is how wide the bell is. That is the width SAC rewards its actor for keeping.
Section four, Listing torques versus outputting them
Figure 4 goes back to the list of torque levels from Section 1.

Try it: the slider sets how many levels each torque is chopped into, and the two buttons switch between the list and the actor. In list mode the grid shows the allowed levels, the bar shows how long the whole list gets over all four torques, the dots trace where the hand has been, and the readout says how often the hand stays on the goal. In actor mode the arrows sit at the exact torque for each joint. Raise the levels and the hand stays on the goal more often, but the bar stays too long to search.

Figure 4 shows the list of torque levels against the actor's exact output. In list mode the grid shows the allowed levels for two torques, the purple bar below it already reads too long to search at three levels per torque, and the readout says the hand stays on the goal rarely. Take sixteen levels: the grid grows denser and the readout turns to often, but the bar still reads too long to search.

Take a look at this figure. In actor mode there is no list between the actor and the motors: each arrow sits at the exact torque the actor outputs for that joint, on a line from minus 1 to 1. The hand traces a smooth curve to the goal instead of stepping between snapped levels. That is what the actor buys: exact torques, and a smooth path.

Figure 5 shows the same arm in actor mode, where no list of levels stands between the actor and the motors. Each line runs from -1 to 1, and each arrow sits at the exact torque the actor outputs for that joint, so the hand traces a smooth curve to the goal instead of stepping between snapped levels. Take the Reacher hand: it stays on the moving goal often, where the list at three levels keeps it there rarely.
Section five, Picking a continuous-action method

This table matches each situation to the method to go to. Each row starts from one situation and ends with the one method that fits it. When each try is costly, as on a real robot, and old steps must be reused, go to SAC: it learns from stored steps, and a wide bell explores through the policy itself, so no noise is added from outside. To learn the ideas on the simplest method, go to DDPG: one actor, one critic, and noise from outside. When DDPG's critic scores too high or training is unstable, go to TD3: two critics, the lower score, and the actor updating half as often. When fresh steps are cheap and simple stable updates matter, go to PPO: small, careful updates from fresh steps only. The pattern: costly tries point to the method that reuses old steps, and unstable training points to the method with the second critic.

Table 2 matches each situation to the method to go to. Each row starts from one situation, a costly try, a first lesson, a critic scoring too high, or cheap fresh steps, and ends with the one method that fits it. Take the row for costly tries: when each try is costly and old steps must be reused, the table points to SAC. SAC learns from stored steps, and a wide bell explores through the policy itself, so no noise is added from outside.
